nodes.label: Taxonomy
nodes.question: What are the three effects mentioned that describe the environmental implications of trade openness?
nodes.answer: The three effects are the scale effect, the composition effect, and the technology effect.
nodes.paragraph: In countries with advanced technological innovation and strong institutional frameworks, trade liberalisation positively impacts environmental quality, whereas the challenge of reducing emissions is more significant in less industrialised nations21. Many scholars affirm that the environmental implications of trade openness vary based on the scale, technique, or composite effects8,15,22 More precisely, free trade has a scale effect because an increased trade volume leads to higher production and energy consumption, resulting in elevated CO2 emissions4,23 In addition, the composition effect suggests that trade increases can affect pollution levels, depending on whether a nation S comparative advantage involves trading goods from energy-intensive sectors. According to the technology effect, trade flows among countries enhance competitiveness, efficiency, and the adoption of environmentally friendly technologies in production, thereby reducing environmental degradation. A recent study by Jahanger24 suggested that the composition effect is the most crucial factor in regulating carbon emissions because the impacts of size and technique are insufficient. Shahzad et al.8 demonstrate that the benefits of improved technologies and effective environmental policies outweigh the negative effects of scale and composition on the environment. Depending on which of the three effects is prominent, the overall impact of trade openness on the environment is unclear, although scale and composition impacts are typically dominant in developing countries.

nodes.question: What is the focus of the paper mentioned in the paragraph?
nodes.answer: The paper analyzes non-cooperative environmental policies in the context of imperfectly competitive environmental industries and transboundary pollution across countries.
nodes.paragraph: (2008), Greaker and Rosendahl (2008), David et al. (2011), Nimubona (2012), Schwartz and Stahn (2014), Fischer et al. (2017, 2018), and Sug- iyama et al. (2023). In these studies, although environmental firms contribute to pol- lution abatement, they cause distortions due to imperfect competition. This paper analyzes non-cooperative environmental policies in the presence of imperfectly competitive environmental industries and transboundary pollution across countries (e.g., greenhouse gases, acid rains, and pollution of shared water resources). The importance of analyzing non-cooperative policymaking under trans- boundary pollution is illustrated by the issue of global climate change. As King and van den Bergh (2021) and others have pointed out, the current initiatives on this issue are a correction of unilateral domestic actions. Under the Paris Agreement, participant countries are supposed to commit themselves to Nationally Determined Contributions (NDCs) for environmental protection. This paper considers a Nash game in taxes and subsidies. In addition to taxes or other emission pricing measures, subsidies are important environmental policy instruments.4 When pollution exter - nalities and imperfect competition exist, efficient policy instruments consist of taxes on polluting firms and subsidies to environmental firms (see David and Sinclair- Desgagn 2010); while taxes correct pollution externalities, subsidies remove the distortion of imperfect competition.5 This paper examines how transboundary pollu- tion distorts these policy choices.

nodes.id: Subtopic:Environment|Climate action|International climate agreements|Multilateral environmental agreements_qna_007
nodes.label: Ethics and regulation
nodes.question: Why is it challenging for countries to cooperate in International Environmental Agreements (IEAs)?
nodes.answer: Cooperation in IEAs is difficult because each country tends to prioritize its self-interest while wanting to participate to reduce pollution and preserve the environment.
nodes.paragraph: International agreements offer a platform for integrating national policies into a global framework. Climate change require long-term strategic policy of each country that can be influenced by the obligations undertaken in international agreements. International agreements provide a frame- work for managing conflicts and tensions between countries and promoting policies that not only address immediate needs but are also sustainable and oriented toward a safer future. Agreements, through cooperation among countries, are fundamen- tal tools to ensure that national policies align with global sustainability, inequality reduction, and resilience goals. Studying these dynamics helps to better understand how international negotiations work, the implementation mechanisms, and the impacts of climate policies on a global scale. During the past three decades, IEAs have been proposed as the only possible solution to control global warming, caused by consumption and production activities among all countries. It is common knowl- edge that cooperation in IEAs is quite difficult to reach because each country would prefer to participate in an agreement in order to reduce pollution and preserve the environment but, at the same time, it would pursue its self interest.

nodes.id: Subtopic:Environment|Climate action|International climate agreements|Multilateral environmental agreements_qna_008
nodes.label: Ethics and regulation
nodes.question: What is required for cooperators to stay in an international environmental agreement (IEA)?
nodes.answer: Cooperators must voluntarily ratify the treaty and stay in the agreement, as there is no supranational authority to enforce environmental policies.
nodes.paragraph: Moreover, all cooperators must voluntarily ratify the treaty and stay in the agreement, due to the absence of a supranational authority that could implement and enforce environmen- tal policies on sovereign countries. An IEA must use the interplay of incentives and interactions among agents to be self-enforcing. The freedom of entrance and depar - ture leads to questions about stability of IEAs. Different game theoretic strands of economic literature have studied the formation and stability of international environ- mental agreements. The non-cooperative approach uses a stability concept proposed by d Aspremont et al. (1983) in the study of cartels, in order to determine the size of a coalition. A coalition is considered to be stable if a signatory is not favourable to leave the agreement (internal stability) and if a non-signatory is not profitable to join the agreement (external stability), assuming that the remaining players do not revise their membership decision. Following Carraro & Siniscalco, (1993), Hoel (1992), de Zeeuw (2008), it is shown that a stable coalition is formed by few countries if they act in a Cournot vein, in contrast, the size of a stable coalition increases if play - ers act in a Stackelberg fashion (see Barrett, 1994; Diamantoudi & Sartzetakis 2006; Rubio & Ulph 2006).

nodes.question: What do the results of the multi-stage game model indicate about adaptation and mitigation decisions?
nodes.answer: The simultaneous decision-making on adaptation and mitigation levels may positively affect the stability of International Environmental Agreements (IEAs).
nodes.paragraph: While mitigation activity is always consid- ered as a public, international good, about adaptation, different scenarios have been proposed. In Lazkano et al. (2016), Rohrer and Rubio (2024) and Benchekroun et al. (2017) adaptation is a private good that only affects the welfare of the host coun- try instead (Masoudi & Zaccour 2017) and Masoudi and Zaccour (2018) assume that adaptation has a public good flavor. In Bayramoglu et al. (2018) it is studied the strategic interaction between mitigation (public good) and adaptation (private good) in a climate agreement. The view that adaptation is a private good is certainly correct when the focus is on the use of a specific adaptation technology. However, new knowledge about adaptation requires investments in research and development (R&D), which can be shared by different entities, with the resulting new technolo- gies benefiting all parties. All paper cited are modelled as a multi-stage game where players select their level of emissions and their level of adaptation in different stages and results indicate that the simultaneous deciding of adaptation and mitigation levels may have a positive effect on the stability of IEAs.

nodes.paragraph: This study indicates a contrasting impact of trade on environmental pollution.
